question.problem:
For the vector $u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $u$ is orthogonal to the set $H=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $u$ is orthogonal to the set $V=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $u$ is orthogonal to the set $W=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\}$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $H,V$ and $W$ as $\{{h}_{1},{h}_{2}\},\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ and $\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\}$, respectively. 

Now, we have to compute the dot product between $u$ and the vectors in each set. 

- For the set $H:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {h}_{1} & =1\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0=-2 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $u$ is not orthogonal to the set $H.$ Notice that we stopped after finding the first non-orthogonal vector in the set.

- For the set $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {v}_{1} & =1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0=0 & ✓ \\ u\cdot {v}_{2} & =1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-2)+2\cdot (-1)=1\ne 0 &  & \times \end{aligned}
$$

 
So, $u$ is not orthogonal to the set $H.$ Notice that, again,  we stopped after finding the first non-orthogonal vector in the set.

- For the set $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {w}_{1} & =1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0=0 & ✓ \\ u\cdot {w}_{2} & =1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (-1)=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $u$ is orthogonal to the set $W.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".
